text: Chapter 2, back-of-the-envelope estimation. In about three minutes, learn how to size a system in a few minutes.

Estimation starts with powers of two. Two to the tenth is about one thousand. Two to the twentieth, about one million. The thirtieth, about one billion. The fortieth, about one trillion, and the fiftieth, about one quadrillion. Every ten bits multiplies the size by roughly a thousand. That gives us kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes, terabytes, and petabytes.

Two mental-math tricks. First, one day is eighty-six thousand four hundred seconds. Just call it ten to the fifth. Second, round your arithmetic too. Ninety-nine thousand nine hundred eighty-seven divided by nine point one? Treat it as one hundred thousand divided by ten. That's ten thousand. Getting the order of magnitude right matters more than the decimals.

Now latency. An L1 cache hit takes half a nanosecond. Main memory, about a hundred nanoseconds. An SSD random read, about a hundred and fifty microseconds. A hard-disk seek, ten milliseconds. A round trip across regions, a hundred and fifty milliseconds. Memory is fast, disk is slow. So avoid disk seeks whenever you can.

Availability is counted in nines. Two nines allow about three point six five days of downtime a year. Three nines, about eight point eight hours. Four nines, about fifty-two minutes. Five nines, about five point three minutes. Six nines, just thirty-one point five six seconds. Each extra nine cuts the downtime budget by a factor of ten.

But three nines per component does not give you three nines end to end. Suppose a request needs the API, the database, and the payment provider, all online at once. The probabilities multiply. Zero point nine nine nine, cubed, is about ninety-nine point seven percent. That's roughly twenty-six hours of downtime a year.

Let's walk through the Twitter example. Three hundred million monthly active users. Half are active daily, so one hundred fifty million. Each posts two tweets a day, giving three hundred million tweets. Divide by eighty-six thousand four hundred seconds: about three thousand five hundred tweets per second on average. Assume peak is double, so about seven thousand per second.

Now storage. One tweet in ten carries media, about one megabyte each. So every day: one hundred fifty million, times two, times ten percent, times one megabyte. That's thirty terabytes. Keep it for five years, multiply by three sixty-five and five: about fifty-five petabytes. And that's raw data only. Replicas and indexes multiply it further.

Averages alone won't save you. Say one instance reliably handles three hundred fifty QPS. At a peak of seven thousand, you need twenty instances. Add thirty percent headroom, and that's about twenty-six. And if users post ten times a day instead of two, QPS grows fivefold. You only change one parameter.
Remember three words: assumptions, units, peak. Write down your assumptions, label your units, never forget the peak. Then go back to the design.
